newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's budget envisions surplus in 2002.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's budget envisions surplus in 2002.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, honoring his pledge to balance the U.S. budget in five years, will unveil a $1.69 trillion spending plan that achieves a $17 billion surplus in 2002, according to a budget summary obtained on Wednesday.
If Congress approved Clinton's budget, spending through 2002 would be $252 billion less than it would be if current policies continued unchanged.

The document projected the deficit would rise in 1997, ending a four-year deficit decline. For the year starting Oct. 1, 1996 the government will run red ink of $125.6 billion, up from the $107.3 billion deficit posted in the previous year and will begin a five-year decline in fiscal 1998 with a deficit of $120.6 billion that year.

To help reach his balanced budget goal, Clinton proposed cuts in the Medicare health program for the elderly, increased fees for use of government services, sales of the broadcast spectrum and a range of changes in government programs from agriculture to job training.
As expected, his budget asked Congress to cut $100 billion over five years from Medicare, the health insurance program for the elderly.

Clinton proposed $98.4 billion in income tax cuts, including a tax credit for children worth $46.0 billion through 2002. If approved by Congress taxpayers would see a $5.5 billion tax break over five years through expanded Individual Retirement Accounts and a $36 billion tax break for education and training.
The much-touted capital gains tax break for sales of homes would be worth $1.4 billion to taxpayers over the five years.

Clinton's budget forecast the economy on a steady growth path of 2.0 percent for 1997 and 1998 and was projected to strenghten to 2.3 percent from 1999 through 2002. Unemployment was expected to reach 5.3 percent in 1997 and then was seen rising to 5.5 percent in 1998. Inflation was forecast at 2.6 percent this year and to rise to 2.7 percent in 1998.

To pay for his policies Clinton proposed to close corporate and investor tax loopholes worth $34.3 billion through 2002, to extend expiring excise and other taxes worth $41.7 billion through 2002. He also expects $36.1 billion will be raised from the sale of broadcast spectrum rights.

While government spending will continue to rise each year through 2002, the White House projects revenues will increase as well to $1.90 trillion in fiscal 2002 from $1.57 trillion expected in fiscal 1998. The government is expected to receive $1.51 trillion in the current 1997 fiscal year.
